---
title: "Figure"
subtitle: "A Figma-style canvas for publication figures, where imported plots stay live"
---

Figure is where figures get built. A project has one or more **canvases** (pages); each canvas
holds **figures** (the framed panels that will appear in your paper); each figure holds
**elements** — imported plots, text, shapes, arrows, images. The key idea:
[plots made with fluxplot stay *live* after import](../concepts/semantic-plots.qmd). Flux
understands their parts, so you can click a single line, axis, or label inside a plot and
restyle it without re-running your analysis — and if you do regenerate the plot, your styling
survives.

# The workspace

- **Tools** use **V** select, **K** scale, **H** hand (pan), **T** text,
  **Alt+R** rectangle, **O** ellipse, **L** line, **Shift+L** arrow, **P** pen.
- **Connectors and labels stick.** A line or arrow drawn from one shape to another sticks to
  both (a dashed outline shows the shape an end will stick to), and dragging one of its ends onto a
  shape sticks that end; a filled end handle marks a stuck end. On a shape the end meets its
  outline, facing the other end; on a plot, an image, a 3D model or a video it stays exactly where
  you released it (hold **Ctrl**/**⌘** as you release to keep the exact spot on a shape too). Move a
  shape and its connectors and labels follow it, live while you drag. A connector never points
  backwards: as the shapes close in it thins out, and while they overlap it is hidden. Any element
  can sit beside another: in the Inspector, **Sticks to** picks the element, the side, the gap and
  the alignment (a line shows **Connector** with its two ends instead); a rotated label sits beside
  it as it looks. Editing a stuck label (its text, bold, size, width or rotation) keeps it stuck;
  moving it by hand frees it, and deleting the shape frees what hung on it. **Settings → Connectors
  stick to shapes** turns the sticking off. From the command line:
  `flux figure-attach <figure> <element> --start A --end B:e:4` (a connector's ends,
  `<id>[:anchor[:gap]]`) or `--to A --side n --gap 8` (beside an element), `--detach` to free it.
  A canvas that holds a stuck element is saved in a newer format, which older Flux versions do not
  open.
- The **sidebar** has two views, **Layers** and **Plots** (the tabs at its top; **Alt+G** goes
  to Plots — see [The Plots rail](#the-plots-rail)). **Layers** lists Canvases (pages — add, rename, delete), Figures on the active canvas
  (family-aware number badges — "2", "S2", "ED3"; double-click opens Figure-Meta’s Name tab), and
  **Layers** — the z-ordered element tree, with per-row show/hide, lock, drag-to-reorder, and
  collapsible groups. Drag its right edge to resize it — as wide as you like, the canvas always
  keeps a strip beside the right rail — and double-click the edge to reset; **Ctrl+B** hides it (bold still wins
  when a text element is selected).
- **Clicking a figure's name takes you to it** — the view centres on that figure at whatever
  zoom you are already working at, so a big canvas stays navigable without hunting. Your zoom
  is never changed for you. Click the name again after panning away to snap back to it.
- **Drag a figure's row up or down the list to reorder the figures** — or press
  **Alt+↑** / **Alt+↓**. **Shift+click** picks a run of rows and **Ctrl+click**
  (**⌘+click** on macOS) adds or drops one, and the whole pick then moves as a block.
  This changes the *order of the list only*: nothing moves on the canvas, and no figure is
  renumbered — reordering and renumbering are separate on purpose, so use Figure-Meta’s Name tab
  below when you want the numbers to follow.
- The **Inspector** puts the selection’s position, size and appearance first. Alignment and
  arrangement tools, the color palette and journal export options can be expanded as needed; drag its left edge to resize it, **Ctrl+Shift+B** hides it for a
  clean canvas.
- **Ctrl+Z** undo, **Ctrl+Shift+Z** redo, zoom controls in the toolbar (5%–25600%).
  Undo and redo buttons show when a step is available. The toolbar distinguishes waiting
  changes, saving, and a failed save with **Retry**. If a save fails, switching between Figure
  and Slide keeps your edits in the original editor until they can be saved.

# Finding and naming figures

Press **Ctrl+K**, choose **New figure**, then click the canvas where its upper-left corner
should go. Flux uses that point when it is free, or the closest position that leaves a small
gap between frames. **Escape** cancels placement. Hold **Alt** while dragging a figure's
title to duplicate the whole figure, including its panels, captions and guides. The copy
inherits its family and receives the next number and a new permanent reference. A click
without a drag creates no copy; **Escape** cancels a duplicate drag and **Ctrl+Z** undoes it.

Selection handles remain usable when an element overhangs its frame. You can also begin a
selection rectangle in the empty canvas outside the active frame and drag across its elements.

Open **All…** in the Figure sidebar, or **Reference, sources & used in…** in the Inspector,
for the project-wide figure catalog. Search by title, designation, reference key, or canvas.
Each result has a preview, source status, and links to the saved documents that use it.
Paper's insert and reference pickers show the same title, designation, canvas, and key.

A figure has three distinct labels:

- **Title** is the human name, such as “Growth curves”. It is the primary label in lists and
  pickers. **Ctrl+R** or a double-click on its sidebar row opens the title editor.
- **Designation** is the publication family and number, such as “Figure 2” or
  “Supplementary Figure 4”. The **Numbering** tab moves a figure within its family; the title
  editor also lets you choose its family (**Alt+↑/↓**) and number. Numbers stay contiguous:
  inserting a number shifts its neighbours, and deletion compacts the surviving figures.
- **Permanent reference** is the stable key, such as `@fig-growth`. Use **Copy** in the catalog
  to copy it. Title changes, numbering changes, canvas moves, and manuscript edits keep that
  key attached to the same figure. Duplicating a figure creates a new key.

**Paper order does not change figures or their numbers.** Reorder prose, references, and
embedded figures freely. Paper displays the numbers chosen in Figure, and exports use those
same numbers. Canvas list order is also separate from publication numbering.

Existing projects retain their reference keys and filenames. The readable title is not a
filename, and you do not need to rename stored files to rename a figure.

# Keeping linked sources current

Select a plot and press **Alt+Shift+C** to copy its full source path. **Ctrl+K → Copy selected
plot path** does the same. A plot imported without a linked source copies the path of its saved
SVG in the project.

Imported plots retain an accepted SVG and its semantic metadata in the project. When analysis
regenerates a linked source, Flux updates that accepted bundle automatically, including changes
only to a manifest or recipe. Figure, Paper, and slides read the accepted version. Edits also
catch up when the project opens and before export. Styling overrides, figure identity, captions,
and deliberate placement scale survive source updates.

The catalog's **Sources** section shows **Linked · current**, **Updating**, **Source missing**,
**Update failed**, or **Frozen version**. A missing or malformed source retains the last good
version; the error explains what needs attention. **Reload sources** retries immediately.
If a saved caption cannot be read, source refresh stops to preserve it. Restore access to
the caption file, then retry **Reload sources**.
**Relink…** chooses a moved source. **Freeze** gives the selected figure an independent saved
version; **Resume updates** links it again. These actions preserve the other figures' links.

**Used in** lists manuscript references and slide copies that share source assets. Removing a
referenced figure or canvas first shows these uses. Paper references then become unresolved;
slide copies retain the assets they need. A slide copy has its own layout and annotations.

# The Plots rail {#the-plots-rail}

The sidebar's **Plots** view keeps your plots beside the canvas while you compose: the
**gallery** on top, and below it the **dissections** of whichever plot you last clicked.

- **Alt+G** shows it and puts the cursor in its search box — it also opens a hidden sidebar.
  Press **Alt+G** again to go back to **Layers**; **Shift+Alt+G** opens
  the full gallery in its own window, from anywhere. Slide mode has the same rail beside its
  slide list ([Slide: the Plots rail](slide.qmd#the-plots-rail)). The two views keep
  their own widths (drag the sidebar's edge), and the canvas stays where it is when you switch.
- **Folders are headings**, not places you go into: every folder of `plots/` is a section
  you scroll through. Click a heading's arrow to fold it (deeper folders start folded);
  **Alt+click** shows that folder alone. Type to search names and folders; **`_`** offers
  the companion collections (`_dissections`, `_lighttable`) — **Enter** goes in,
  **Backspace** in an empty search comes back out. **Proj** / **Glob** (**Alt+1** /
  **Alt+2**) switch between this project and your global plot library.
- **Alt+/** switches the lower pane between Dissections and **Folders**. The tree shows the
  plot folders and how many plots each holds, with a search box for finding a nested
  directory. Choose a folder to show only its plots; **↑/↓**, **←/→**, and **Enter** navigate
  and choose from the tree. The folder stays chosen while you flip to Layers and back.
  Companion directories stay out of this tree. Use **Alt+/** again to return to dissections.
- Plots sit at their true shape, several to a row, and every one is drawn on a background
  chosen so **all of it shows**: dark ink on paper, white ink (a plot made for a dark slide)
  on dark, both on grey, and a plot's own paper colour when it declares one. The **⋯** menu
  can set the background yourself (paper, dark, a checkerboard, or the figure's own), sort
  **Recent first** (newest-changed plots on top), and hide names. **Tiles → Gallery** and
  **Tiles → Dissections** size each part separately (or **Ctrl+wheel** over it; **Reset
  sizes** goes back to 112 and 84 px).
- Small marks on a tile: **●** the plot is placed in the active figure (dimmer: placed
  elsewhere in the project, with a count); **⧉ 12** it has 12 dissection files (click it to
  show them); **◆** an editable fluxplot. A dashed outline marks the plot selected on the
  canvas, and the rail scrolls to it (switch that off in **⋯**). An accent **dot** marks a
  plot that is new or was regenerated since the rail last listed it — handy after a re-run
  of your analysis; clicking the plot clears it, and **⋯ → Clear the new-file dots** clears
  them all. **⋯ → Width class badge** adds the journal width each plot will print at:
  **1c** (one column, up to about 90 mm), **1.5c**, **2c** (full page, about 180 mm).
- **Rest the pointer on a plot** for a moment to **peek** at it: a larger picture beside the
  rail with its full name and folder, its printed size (in inches, as for matplotlib's
  `figsize`; **Settings → Figure → Physical sizes** switches Peek and the Inspector to
  millimetres) and width class, when it changed,
  where it is placed, its dissection folders, and why its tile has the background it has.
  If the plot's ink would read poorly on the active figure's background, Peek says so.
  **Shift+Space** peeks at the selected tile from the keyboard (and closes it again). Peek
  never takes clicks and vanishes when the pointer leaves the rail; **⋯ → Peek on hover**
  turns the hover off.
- **Narrow the gallery** from **⋯ → Show only**: **Unused** (in no figure yet — slides are not counted),
  **Fluxplots** (editable ones), **Has dissections**. Active filters show as chips under the
  search box; click one to remove it. Right-click a plot (or a folder heading) for **Show
  only this folder**, and **Backspace** in an empty search climbs back out one folder at a
  time. **Similar names** lists a plot's variants across all folders (`_v2`, `_s07`, …), even
  from inside a folder shown alone; **Escape** returns to where you were.
- **⋯ → Stack variants** folds runs of variants in one folder — `fig1_a` … `fig1_f`,
  `latency`, `latency_v2` … — into one tile showing the newest, with a **×6** badge.
  **Enter**, a double-click or the badge opens the stack in place; the first variant's
  **◂** badge folds it again. Dragging a stack places the variant it shows.
- While you work, Flux prepares the previews of the plots you have not scrolled to yet, a
  little at a time, so the next scroll or project open is instant. It pauses while you drag
  on the canvas, leaves very large files (over 2 MB) until you scroll to them, and stops for
  the session if a file crashes the preview renderer.
- **Double-click** or **Enter** places the selected plots in the figure named at the top
  (**→ Fig 3** — click it to pick another figure). **Drag** a plot onto any figure to place
  it where you let go; over the canvas it shows at the size it will land. **Space** opens a
  full-window preview. **Ctrl+Z** undoes a placement without leaving the rail. Typing
  anywhere in the rail goes to its search box, so tool keys never change your tool by
  accident.
- **Dissections** follow your clicks — a plot clicked in the gallery or on the canvas. Tables
  come first as small previews (a one-row statistics table reads as a list), then each folder
  of panels; very large folders show a few and **Show all**. If you were looking at a file
  (say `by_subject/s07`) and click another plot with the same file, it stays selected in the
  same place, so you can compare subjects plot to plot. Clicking an empty spot keeps the last
  plot showing; the **pin** keeps it while you click elsewhere. **Double-click**, **Enter** or
  **Space** opens a file in the Dissect viewer; drag a panel onto a figure to place it.
- **Notes** in Dissections lets you create and edit ordinary `.txt` companions with **+ Note**.
  A plot can have several named notes. They save as you type; **Ctrl+S** saves now.
  The full Dissect viewer has the same **Notes** control. To search their contents across the
  project, switch on **Notes** beside the gallery search and type a word or tag such as
  `#TODO`; choose a match to select its plot and open the note here. If another writer changed
  a note, Flux keeps your draft and explains the conflict before replacing anything.
- Drag the line between the two parts to share the height; drag it to an edge to fold a
  part away; double-click it to reset. Files that appear or change in `plots/` show up on
  their own.

# Getting plots in

- The toolbar's **Gallery** opens the full **Plot gallery** (**Shift+Alt+G** opens it in its
  own window), showing SVG and PNG previews in the current
  folder, including GLB meshes marked **3D**. Choose **Gallery** or **List**; adjust **Size**, **Space**, and **Names** to make
  the contact sheet comfortable. Size reaches **800 px** for large previews. **Folders**
  shows or collapses a directory tree; clicking a folder shows what is in it, and the **›**
  arrow beside it expands or collapses its branches, so you can browse files without losing
  your picks (**Settings → Plot gallery** can make the click do both). Flux remembers these
  display choices.
- **Project** / **Global** at the top of the gallery (**Alt+1** / **Alt+2**) switches between
  this project's `plots/` folder and your **global plot library**, the
  `plot_library` folder inside your FluxConfig folder (by default
  `~/FluxConfig/plot_library`). Put plots you reuse everywhere there, such as logos,
  schematics, reference panels and colour keys. Organise it with any folders you like, as
  you would a project's `plots/`; Flux creates the folder the first time you open **Global**
  and **Open folder** takes you there. Picks from both scopes can go in together. The
  project keeps its own copy of every plot you insert, and a global plot stays linked to its
  file in the library, so regenerating it there updates it here on this machine. The global
  library holds SVG, PNG and GLB plots; video clips live in a project's `plots/_videos/`.
- **What a search covers** is set in **Settings → Figure → Plot gallery**: everything in
  the scope you are browsing (the default), only the current folder and its subfolders, only
  project plots, only global plots, or everything in both. When results come from outside
  the scope you are browsing, each one is labelled **Project** or **Global**.
- Click a plot, or press **Enter** or **Space** in an empty search box, to select it.
  Picks survive folder changes and searches. **Ctrl+Enter**, the **Insert** button, or
  a double-click inserts the selection. By default, search reaches ordinary folders
  throughout the tree you are browsing. The root button (**plots** or **plot_library**)
  returns to the top, and **Up** or **Backspace** goes to the parent folder.
- **Ctrl-click** (Mac: **⌘-click**) a plot, or use **Preview** / **F4**, for a full-window
  view. Arrow keys browse adjacent plots; **Escape** returns to the gallery. Open
  **Dissections** or press **D** to inspect the plot's companion groups and panels.
  **Similar names** finds filename variants across the current search scope, without
  selecting them. Clear that filter to return to normal browsing.
- **Pin open** moves the gallery into its own resizable window. Move it to another screen
  and keep arranging figures in the editor. The current folder and selection are preserved,
  and you can still browse the entire `plots/` tree and the global library. Insertions leave the window open and
  use the figure named in its footer. Successful insertions clear the submitted picks,
  ready for the next batch. **Dock** returns the same gallery to the editor;
  **Alt+G** brings an already pinned gallery forward. **Refresh** reloads files and previews.
  Preview columns adjust as you resize the pinned window, including while the editor is
  minimized. Closing the project also closes its gallery.
- **◆** marks semantic plots and **◇** marks plain images; **List** also shows semantic
  and paper-snip badges. The reserved [`_dissections/`](../concepts/dissections.qmd) and
  `_lighttable/` companion collections stay out of ordinary results. Type **`_`** to list
  them and **Enter** to go in, or open them in **Folders**. Search then stays inside that
  collection until you leave it. The Slide gallery also previews MP4/MOV clips: select
  **Play video** to play, pause, seek, or mute a clip in the full-window view.
- **Drag files in** from your file manager (an SVG with its `.fluxplot.json` sibling imports
  as a semantic plot), or **paste an image** straight from the clipboard. A pasted image has
  no file behind it, so Flux keeps the original for you in
  [`plots/pasted/`](../reference/project-layout.qmd).
- Everything imports at **true physical size** — a 6.4 × 4.8 inch plot lands exactly that
  big, never silently rescaled. If an import is larger than its figure frame, a toast says so:
  **Ctrl+Shift+I** brings the selection inside the frame (moving it, never resizing it).

# 3D models and 3D fluxplots {#3d-models}

Import a **GLB** mesh through **Import**, drag it onto the canvas, or pick its **3D** tile in
the gallery. Flux keeps a project copy, so sharing the project does not depend on the
original file. A plain GLB supplies geometry and colours. A **3D fluxplot** also supplies
named parts, physical size, axes, labels, value fields and optional shapes through the
matching `.fluxplot.json` file. Keep that file beside the GLB when importing. An invalid,
newer or mismatched manifest produces a warning and leaves the geometry available as a
plain mesh.

3D models need a saved project. In a project you have not saved yet, importing a GLB first
asks you to save it; then the file picker opens again, so pick the files a second time.
Cancelling that second picker keeps the saved project. Dragged-in files need no second
pick. If preparing a model takes more than a second, a notice names the files still being
imported. A placed model shows a dashed outline while its image is prepared, and
“Preparing 3D preview” only if that takes longer than a second.

In Python, start a scene, add your mesh and save it into `plots/`. This needs a fluxplot
version with 3D support (`fp.scene3d`), which is not in a fluxplot release yet.

```python
import fluxplot as fp

# vertices is an N×3 array; faces is an M×3 array of vertex indices.
sc = fp.scene3d(figsize=(3.5, 3), units="µm", up="z", axes="triad")
fp.mesh3d(sc, (vertices, faces), series="neuron", color="#4385be")
sc.view(azimuth=30, elevation=20)
fp.save(sc, "plots/neuron")
```

`figsize` is in inches; `up` describes your data coordinates. The gallery inserts that
physical size. In a trusted notebook, displaying `sc` opens the interactive viewer.
Use **Copy view** and paste the `sc.view(...)` line it produces into your code, then save to
make that angle the scene's Home view. In the viewer, click the model (or hold **Ctrl**) before
scrolling to zoom; otherwise scrolling moves the notebook as usual. For a static output, use `sc.show(static=True)`.

After rerunning Python, **Source changed** appears in the Inspector and as a dot in
Layers, together with **Update from source**. Choose it to accept the new geometry and
metadata. Your box, camera and look stay in place; restyles and field settings remain for
surviving part IDs, and shape weights remain for surviving names. Flux warns when parts
disappear or bounds move substantially. **Undo** restores the previous stored model.
Source changes never replace the model automatically. A missing original file leaves the
saved copy available. For a recipe-backed model, **Regenerate** in X-ray reruns the recipe
with its parameters and applies the same update after it succeeds.

**Double-click the mesh**, or choose **Orbit** in the Inspector, to turn it. While you
orbit, the button reads **Done** and a hint over the model lists the keys:

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **Drag** | Orbit around the model |
| **Shift+drag** | Pan within the model's box |
| **Alt+drag** | Roll the camera |
| **Wheel** | Zoom the model |
| **←** **→** **↑** **↓** | Turn the view in 5° steps (**Shift** for 15°) |
| **1**–**6** | The six axis views, as on the Inspector's view buttons |
| **0** | Home view and saved shape weights |
| **P** | Switch orthographic / perspective |
| **Enter** | Finish, like **Done**; one **Undo** restores the previous view |
| **Esc** | Cancel the whole orbit visit |

Clicking outside the model also finishes. **Space+drag** and **Ctrl+wheel** return to
canvas navigation. Double-clicking a label, colorbar, legend or scale bar selects that part
instead, as with a 2D plot's parts.

The Inspector's **3D model** panel is grouped into sections:

- **3D view**: **Orbit**, the camera numbers, the view buttons **Front**, **Back**,
  **Right**, **Left**, **Top**, **Bottom** and **Home** (each shows its key), and
  **Projection** (**Ortho** or **Persp**).
- **Appearance**: **Colours** is **From file** (the mesh's own colours) or **Uniform** (one
  **Model colour**, shown only for Uniform); **Lighting** is **Studio** or **Unlit**.
- **Value fields** and **Shape**, when the model has them (see below).

Resizing the box reframes the model while labels keep their physical type size. A physical
scale bar is shown only in orthographic view. The default view fits the model snugly; with
box axes it fits the whole axes box, so ticks and labels stay inside the frame. Looking
almost straight down one axis shrinks it to a short stub. Its tick labels are then hidden
rather than stacked on top of each other, and so is its title if the title is longer than
the stub. The axis line, ticks and grid stay.

Use **R** for the model's **X-ray**. Named mesh parts can be recoloured, hidden or made
transparent; labels can be restyled independently. Mesh-part colours show while **Colours**
is **From file**, so painting a mesh part on a Uniform model switches it to From file (one
undo, with a notice). For a continuous value field, change its colormap and **Min / Max** under
**Value fields**: the mesh and colorbar update together, without rerunning Python. A part
colour overrides its value field; **Reset part colour** restores field colouring.

If the GLB has named shape states, **Shape** offers live weights from 0 to 1. A sequence
instead starts with a **Frame** control: 0 is the base, 1 onwards are the saved shapes,
and fractional values blend neighbouring frames. **Custom** means the current weights
are not a sequence frame. **Reset shape** restores the saved weights. Stored scientific
weights can extend beyond the slider range.

PNG and TIFF exports rasterize the result at the requested print size. SVG and PDF keep
the mesh as a high-resolution image while axes, labels, legends and scale bars remain
vector artwork. Paper uses the saved figure view in its embeds and document exports.
Large meshes can be reduced at creation with `fp.mesh3d(..., max_faces=...)`; this uses
the optional `fluxplot[mesh]` extra. Texture images are omitted and skinning is ignored:
Flux shows the stored mesh geometry, so bake a desired pose before exporting the GLB.
Point and line primitives are refused; export triangle meshes.

# Selecting inside plots

Selection follows Figma's logic, tuned for plots:

- A **plain click** (or drag) anywhere on a plot always takes the **whole plot** — you can
  use empty space inside its rectangular bounds even when the SVG background is transparent.
  You can never accidentally drag one bar out of a chart.
- **Ctrl+click** pierces to the exact **part** under the cursor — a series' line, one point, an
  axis label — even on an unselected plot. Hold **Ctrl** and hover to preview what you'd get;
  a data part also shows its **readout** beside the box — a point's x and y, a bar's category
  and height, a hexagon's count, a heatmap cell's value, a box's statistics, a significance
  bracket's test and p — read from the plot's manifest, never from the picture.
- **Double-click** descends a level: into a group, into a plot's parts, into text editing,
  into a path's nodes.
- **Ctrl+Shift+click** adds the part under the cursor to the pick (click it again to drop it).
  Once a plot has a picked part, a plain **Shift+click** on another of its parts adds that one
  too — so Ctrl+click the first point, Shift+click the rest. Every picked part is outlined.
- **Ctrl+drag** from a plot's empty space draws a **marquee inside the plot**: every part that
  ends up fully inside the box is picked — the same box you draw in the slide **Become**
  picker. Data marks win over furniture (a box around three points and the tick labels under
  them picks the points), and when no data mark is inside the furniture is picked. Hold
  **Shift** as well to add to what you already have; **Escape** mid-drag drops the box.
- Whatever you've picked stays plain-draggable — drag any picked part and the whole pick moves
  together (**Shift** locks the axis), the arrow keys nudge them all — and **Escape** steps
  back out one level at a time.

With a part selected, press **F** to open **Properties** and restyle it — color, width, size, font, opacity, visibility,
even a positional nudge in the plot's own units. The same fields sit in the right rail's
**Plot part** section. Part edits are stored as overrides keyed to the part's stable name, so
**they survive regeneration** of the plot. Recolouring a series' whole line or points repaints its
legend swatch too, so the key never lies about the colour; recolouring one bar or one point is a
highlight and leaves the key alone.

When the picked part belongs to a plain series, the **Plot part** section also offers **Series
colour**: one colour for the whole series — its line, its markers' faces and edges, its bars or
band, its error bars and its legend swatch — written as one override per part, so it survives
regeneration like any part edit, with **reset** to return to the generated colours. A
colour-mapped series (a heatmap, a hexbin, a scatter coloured by value) has no series colour: edit
its **Colour scale** instead. The headless twin is `set-series-color`.

**R** opens the **X-ray**: the anatomy of the selected plot (or group) as a tree, placed
beside the selection. Walk it with the arrow keys, hide/show any part with **x**, press
**Enter** (or **F**) to select the picked parts and open their properties, and — for recipe-backed
plots — hit **Regenerate** to re-run the script that made it, right from the panel. Rows
**multi-select**: **Shift+click** picks a run, **Ctrl+click** (Mac **⌘+click**) toggles one,
**Ctrl+A** picks everything, **Alt+A** picks every search result, and a press-and-drag over
rows picks the run you sweep (hold **Ctrl** when you press to add a second sweep to the pick).
**a** widens the pick to its siblings: first the same part under each sibling of its parent —
*X axis › Tick marks* adds *Y axis › Tick marks* — then, pressed again, every row under the same
parent. **x**, **Enter** and the property menu then act on all of them — hide five series at
once, or restyle them together. Select **several plots** before
pressing **R** and the X-ray shows each plot's tree plus a **Common parts** list of
what they all share, so hiding the x-axis of four plots is one row and one keypress.
**Double-click** a row (or **Ctrl+Enter**) to re-root the X-ray on it. Keyboard navigation
keeps the active row in view. You can inspect another plot while a recipe runs; its result
still belongs to the plot you regenerated.

Every row says what it is without a hover. Search results and common parts carry their place —
*X axis › Tick labels*, *Y axis › Tick marks*, *Panel b › Colorbar* — and, on the right, what
they show: tick values (*0 · 800 · 1600 · 2400*), an axis's title, a series' kind, size and
colour. A common part whose value differs between the plots reads *varies*. With several plots, each
plot row and search header is named by what sets it apart (the part of the file names they all
share is shown once, on the *N plots* row: *…bandpower-* → **low-gamma**), beside its title and a
tiny map of the figure with that plot lit, so you can tell "the bottom-left one" at a glance;
search results gather under those headers. Search matches words
anywhere in a row's place and value: *x tick* finds only the x axes' ticks, *y lab* the y tick
labels, *sigma tick* that plot's ticks, *SWS* the tick label that reads it. A small dot marks a
restyled part (hollow: something inside it), **◐** a partly hidden one, and a series shows its
colour. The strip above the
buttons describes the row under the pointer (else the picked one) in full: its whole path,
its values or data readout, its kind, effective style, what is restyled or hidden and its part id.
Hovering a row outlines its parts on the canvas — on every plot, for a common part.

A group's members are rows too: open *Tick labels* to see each tick label and its text (big
groups show their first 60, then **+ N more**). **Ctrl+click** one tick label on the canvas and
press **R**: the X-ray opens on it. **←** then steps up to its family — all the tick labels —
and **→** back down; **Shift+Alt+R** opens on the family directly, and selects it on the canvas.
**Shift+A** takes the picked part to every plot in the figure that has it (the X-ray re-roots on
those plots with the part picked on all of them; **⌫** comes back). Hiding a family with **x**
hides all of it; showing one member inside a hidden family shows just that member. **Ctrl+Z**
undoes without closing the X-ray.

# Dissecting a plot

A summary plot usually hides a story — twenty subjects behind one regression line, a table
of statistics behind one asterisk. **D** with a plot selected opens **Dissect**: a viewer for
that plot's *companion material*, which lives in
[`plots/_dissections/<plot name>/`](../concepts/dissections.qmd). Drop per-subject panels,
alternative analyses, or stats CSVs there (subfolders become tabs) and they're one keypress
away from the composed figure — without ever appearing in the plot importer or your figures.

Inside the viewer: **arrow keys** move around the grid, **Enter** expands a file
(**Ctrl+scroll** zooms images at the cursor, **Space+drag** pans, **Enter** toggles fit/1:1),
CSV and TSV files open as sortable tables, and **Esc** steps back out. The **⧉** button
shrinks the viewer to a floating window you can keep beside the canvas; files dropped into
the folder while it's open appear live. The Inspector's **Dissections** button (with a count)
does the same as **D** — and for a plot with no dissections yet, it offers to create the
folder.

# Everyday editing

In the Figure and Slide editors the pointer is Flux's own: by default a **classic arrow** in
Figma's style — a pink, slightly leaning arrowhead with a deep indigo outline and a faint lift — and
it is one mark that changes form rather than a set of unrelated system arrows: over an object's
edge or corner it becomes a double-headed resize arrow drawn in the same fill and outline, just
outside a corner a curved rotate arrow, with a small **+** while **Alt** is duplicating, and it
keeps that form for the whole drag. Paper, Reader and Library keep the system's cursors; text
fields keep the I-beam and pan keeps the hand. **Settings → General → Cursor** tunes the arrow —
its fill and outline colours, size, outline width, corner rounding, shadow and tilt — with a live
preview. **Press on click** adds a subtle tip-led depression on the canvas, holding while the
button is down and returning on release. **Press depth** adjusts the travel and shadow compression;
The default depth is **1.25×**. **Return time** adjusts how quickly it lifts back (80 ms by default). Use **Click to try the press**
to feel changes in Settings, or turn **Press on click** off to keep the arrow still.
The cursor style can also switch to the **crosshair**: a precise cross with a gap at the centre so the pixel
you point at is never covered, whose colour follows the surface (dark ink over paper and other
light surfaces, paper-white over the dark canvas and chrome, flipping over dark fills and
dark-theme plots), with its own colours, stroke, optional halo, centre mark, hover dot and press
contraction, and Adaptive, Outlined and Accent presets. Either style can hand the resize, rotate
and move states back to the system's own cursors.

**Selecting and moving.** Click an object to select it; a path, line or hollow shape is
selected by clicking on or near its stroke. Once selected, its **bounding box is the handle**:
drag from anywhere inside the box — an open path's empty interior, a hollow ellipse's middle,
the gaps of a group, even over a plot the path annotates — to move it, and a click there keeps
it selected (a click on an object lying beneath the selection selects that object instead; an
object drawn on top of the selection still wins its own click). A drag has to travel a few
pixels before anything moves, so a shaky click never nudges. With several objects selected, a
click on one of them selects just that one; a drag still moves them all.

**Resizing and rotating.** The selection shows four corner handles. Drag a **corner** to resize
both axes, or grab **anywhere along an edge** to resize that axis alone — the edge follows your
drag from wherever you took hold of it, and snaps to neighbouring edges, centres and guides
the way a move does. **Shift** keeps the proportions (from an edge it grows about the opposite
edge's middle), **Alt** resizes about the centre (press or release it mid-drag and the box
follows at once), and the live **W × H** readout under the box shows the size as you go.
Thin objects — a scale bar, a one-line label — have no edge bands across their short side, so
their whole body stays grabbable; their corners still resize them from the outside. To
rotate, drag the knob above the box or simply drag from **just outside any corner**;
**Shift** snaps to 15°. **Ctrl+drag** a handle or edge of an image or plot to crop instead
(on a plot, **Ctrl** just inside the edge still picks the part under the pointer). Images and
plots resize freely by an edge, so use a corner or **Shift** when the proportions matter.

Drag to move (with smart snapping and alignment guides), arrows to nudge, **Alt+drag** to
duplicate, **Shift+drag** to constrain to an axis. To move something to a **different
figure**, just drag it there: the figure under the pointer lights up, and releasing puts the
selection into that figure where you dropped it (groups and panel captions come along; one
Undo brings it back). **Ctrl+X** cuts, **Ctrl+C** copies and **Ctrl+V** pastes, so a cut in
one figure and a paste in another is the keyboard way to do the same thing. **Ctrl+G** groups
(**Ctrl+Shift+G** ungroups), **]** brings to front and **[** sends to back (with **Ctrl** they
move one step), **Shift+H** / **Shift+V** flip, **Delete** removes, **Escape** cancels whatever
you're midway through. The Inspector's Align row lines selections up, distributes them, and
sets exact gaps.

Press **F** with anything selected for the **property menu** — the fastest way to edit, built
for one hand on the keyboard and one on the mouse. It opens **beside the selection**, never on
top of it (when nothing fits, it takes the side that covers the least), and lays its groups
out in narrow columns — each row is a key and a name over its control — so nothing scrolls.
Opening a larger picker repositions the menu when needed to keep the selection clear.
Every hotkey is a **left-hand key** (`1`–`6`, `q w e r t`, `a d g`, `z x c v b`; `h` for a
plot's **content scale** or a text's **letter spacing**, and `n` for **paragraph spacing**),
so the right
hand never leaves the wheel: press the key to **arm** the row, then roll the **mouse wheel**
anywhere on the screen to adjust it (a slow roll moves one step per notch, a flick moves fast,
a trackpad scrubs; **Shift** ×10, **Alt** ×0.1; **↑/↓** step too, typed digits replace), and
press **Space** or **Enter** to apply — **Escape** reverts. A choice such
as font or alignment expands its options inline (wheel, **w/a/s/d**, **1–9**, or click); a
colour opens the **palette** — every row on one line, the whole grid in view — with the
full **spectrum** beside it (a saturation/value square and a hue bar, seeded from the current
colour), a hex field and an **eyedropper**; hovering a swatch previews it live, a click
applies it, and a drag on the square previews until you let go. The hex field and spectrum
follow the preview. The opacity slider under the spectrum is the *picked paint's* own
opacity — a fill picker sets the fill's, a stroke picker the stroke's (a text colour sets the
object's opacity) — and shows the selection's current value (or **mixed**).
Releasing the hue or opacity slider applies that adjustment and keeps the picker open so
you can continue tuning the colour.
The eyedropper samples a colour from your screen. On Linux it uses your desktop's
colour picker; **Escape** cancels without changing your artwork. If screen picking
is unavailable, Flux offers a magnified view labelled **Pick from Flux window**,
which samples only this window. A completed pick is one undoable change.
**Escape** or clicking outside dismisses an unchosen preview; an incomplete hex stays editable
until you finish it. The palette comes in
**collections** — Flexoki (the default), ColorBrewer, Paul Tol's colour sets, and your
project's own imported palette — as tabs above the grid; **Shift+Tab** cycles them. **Tab**
switches the grid to the **colormaps**: every map fluxplot ships (matplotlib, Crameri's
Scientific colour maps, Paul Tol, cmasher), by collection and by type, each with a preview
bar — pick a map and hover along its bar to take the colour at that position, **r** reverses
it. Or take the *whole* map: **x** or **y** (or the *along x* / *along y* buttons under the bar)
lays it across the element as a **gradient** along that axis — x left→right, y bottom→top — for
a shape's fill or stroke, a line's or arrow's stroke (arrowheads included), or a text's glyphs.
The map's colours are stored on the element itself, so the gradient travels into every export
(SVG, PNG, TIFF), headless render and exported deck exactly as drawn;
the menu chip and the Inspector swatch show the map and name it (`crameri.batlow · along y`),
and picking any plain swatch returns the element to a solid colour. Plot *parts* take solid
colours only. Settings → Figure chooses which palette and colormap collection a picker opens on. Hovering any numeric row and rolling the wheel edits it directly, so
the menu works with the mouse alone as well; **s** searches the properties. It carries the
essentials (position, size with **aspect lock**, rotation, opacity) plus the deep cuts: dashed
strokes with dash/gap control, **arrowheads** on lines *and* open paths (filled or V-line,
sized, with round/flat/square caps), **corner radius** on rectangles *and* paths,
no-fill/no-stroke, separate **fill opacity** (**b**) and **stroke opacity** (**t**) — each
independent of the object's **opacity**, which multiplies both — text styling — and **save as
preset** for anything you want to reuse. The
right rail carries the same properties (fill, stroke and text colours with their palette
names, sizes, stroke widths, arrowheads), so the menu is a choice, not a requirement.

Numeric fields accept expressions such as `240/2` and display fractional values even when
the normal wheel increment is a whole unit. Drag a field’s label to scrub, or click
its input and type. A scrub or a continuous text/property edit is one undo step; **Escape**
cancels the current preview. Mixed selections show **Mixed** and how many objects a property
can change. Locked or hidden objects, including members of a locked or hidden group, stay
unchanged while you edit the rest of a selection.

In **Layers**, **Ctrl/⌘+click** toggles objects and **Shift+click** selects a range. With a row
focused, **↑/↓** moves through the list, **Home/End** reaches either end, **Shift+↑/↓** extends
the selection, and **F2** renames. A group opens or closes with **→/←**. Locks inherited from
a parent group explain which group must be unlocked.

# Resizing a figure

Click the figure’s title above its frame, then drag an edge or corner of the frame. The
handles stay the same size on screen as you zoom. **Shift** preserves the frame’s original
aspect ratio. The Inspector shows the new dimensions during the drag; **Escape** restores
the original boundary, and a completed resize is one undo step.

Resizing the frame changes the export boundary. Your plots, text and shapes retain their
size and world position. Moving a left or top edge moves the boundary around the artwork;
elements and ruler guides adjust their local coordinates to stay in place. Artwork outside
the new frame remains in the project and reappears if you enlarge the boundary again.
Dragging the title still moves the whole figure. Slides use a shared deck stage size.

## Resizing a plot

Plots saved with fluxplot 0.4 or later include measured layout information. Drag a plot's
edge or corner, or type its width and height in the Inspector, to **Reflow** it: axes and data
areas change size, numeric ticks are recomputed, and text, strokes and markers keep their
physical point sizes. **Native size** restores the dimensions from Python. A deliberate
size chosen in Flux survives regeneration; an untouched plot follows the new Python size.

Legends use fewer columns when they need more room, keeping their labels and swatches at
their original size where possible. A legend that still cannot fit shrinks together with its
frame; a titled legend keeps its composition and shrinks as a unit. Returning to a wider plot
restores the original legend layout.

Hiding plot parts in **X-ray** tightens the selection and hover outline around the remaining
visible content. The plot keeps its saved dimensions, so showing those parts restores its
original frame. Selection, dragging and resize previews use the visible bounds; cropping
continues to work against the saved plot frame.

The Layout controls offer **Stretch** for the previous resize behavior. The status line
explains whether the result is exact, reflowed, approximate, or stretching, with a reason.
Legacy plots need one regeneration to enable reflow. Polar plots, 3D, subfigures, compressed
layout and unsupported transforms use Stretch with a named reason. Date, category and custom
ticks keep their source positions and labels. Extremely small sizes may crowd decorations;
enlarge the plot when the status reports this.

**Content scale** (or the **K** scale tool) changes the physical size of text, strokes and
markers within the chosen box. Crop boundaries remain figure fractions during reflow.
Pictures without text or lines, such as a PNG inside an SVG, have nothing for content scale
to change, so the Inspector explains this instead of showing the field.

Select several reflow-capable plots and use **Match plot area → Width / Height / Both** in
Arrange to match their data areas. The anchor pin is the reference when selected; otherwise
the first selected plot is the reference. This is one undo step. Then **Align plot areas**
can align their reflowed spines. Aspect constraints and infeasible sizes are reported.
A single panel picked in X-ray scopes that plot's data area for Match; other selected plots
use their full panel union. Locked or excluded plots cannot be changed by Match.

## Axis view

Select a plot with a manifest containing series and calibrated axes to edit **Axis view** in
the Object inspector. The controls are unavailable without axes and series; an unsupported axis
is disabled with its reason. Each supported axis has **min** and **max**
in data units and a **linear/log** scale. An empty field uses the generated plot's limit,
shown as its placeholder. **Reset** restores both generated axes. Typing or wheeling previews
the change; finishing the edit makes one undo step, and **Escape** cancels it.

The **F** menu offers **x view** (**v**) and **y view** (**b**); on cropped plots, follow the
row's displayed key when **v** is already assigned. Once a view is open there, the mouse wheel
adjusts the focused limit wherever the pointer is (the canvas does not zoom); **Space** accepts
the minimum and moves to the maximum, and **Space** again (or **Enter**) accepts it and returns to
the menu. In X-ray, select an axis row and press
**v** for **Axis view…** to focus that axis in the Inspector.

Lines, points, bars, heatmap cells, hexagons, contour bands and box or violin bodies re-project
inside the existing plot frame; exports include the same view. A viewed axis is re-ticked: its
generated ticks, labels and gridlines give way to a fresh set laid out for the new limits (nice
steps with matching labels on a linear axis, decades on a log one; an axis of categories, dates
or fixed labels keeps its own ticks, which move with their values and fade in the outer 4%).
Non-series marks, such as a dashed reference line, and raster layers stay put. A log view needs
positive limits and positive data. For multi-panel plots the view applies to all panels;
placeholders show the first panel.

A plot with a **twin value axis** (an `ax.twinx()` or `twiny()` in fluxplot 0.3.2 or later) shows
a **y2** (or **x2**) row too: the twin's own limits and scale, applied to the series drawn on it
while the panel's other series stay where they are. A secondary axis that only relabels its
parent through a function follows the parent and has no row of its own.

## Colour scales

A colour-mapped plot saved by fluxplot 0.3.1 or later (hexbin, heatmap, scatter with `c=`,
contour bands, colour-mapped bars and lines) records each colour scale's exact law — its colormap
table, its normalisation and limits — and every coloured element's data value. Select the plot to
edit **Colour scales** in the Object inspector, one block per scale. In the **F** menu, the
**colour scale** row opens the editor with the whole menu to itself, widened to fit: the
controls on the left and the palette list always open on the right, so trying palettes is one
click (or **↑/↓** and **Enter**) each; **Esc** returns to the other properties. The X-ray widens
while its palette list is open, and a wide list shows each type's maps in two columns. The **palette** takes any
colormap fluxplot ships, typed by name or picked from the collections behind the preview bar;
**Reverse** flips it; the **norm** kind offers the kinds the scale allows (linear, log, power,
symlog; a centre appears for two-slope norms, gamma for power, the linear threshold and scale
for symlog); **min** and **max** are data units; **extend** chooses which out-of-range arrows
the key shows. Every element recolours as you type, together with the key's gradient and its
ticks, and nothing regenerates. An empty field uses the generated value shown as its
placeholder; finishing an edit makes one undo step, **Escape** cancels it and **Reset** restores
the generated scale. An edit that cannot be painted, such as a log minimum at zero or a minimum
above the maximum, is refused with its reason and the plot keeps the last valid colours. A scale
that also carries an **opacity channel** (fluxplot's `alpha_by`: a hexagon's count, a cell's
p-value) keeps every element's opacity through a recolour; the block names the channel and its
range, and it is edited in the source.

Live edits are element state: they are saved with the figure, honoured by exports and Paper
embeds, tween in slides and travel with copies of the plot. **Apply to source** writes the
complete colour controls of every scale into the plot's recipe, regenerates the plot from its
data and clears the live edit, so the source file paints the same colours; it needs a runnable
recipe. A scale drawn as one raster image reports itself and can only regenerate. Older plots
without a recorded scale keep the regenerate-only palette and range fields.

The **F** menu offers **colour scale** (**c**, or the key the row displays) with the same
controls, and X-ray shows them under the plot's regenerate controls. The headless twin is
`set-plot-color-scale` (see the Slide mode chapter).

## View as

**View as…** in the toolbar shows the whole canvas the way a colour-deficient reader sees it —
**deuteranopia**, **protanopia**, **tritanopia** (Machado 2009 at full severity, the same
simulation fluxplot's accessibility lint uses) — or in **greyscale** (luminance, what a black-and-
white print keeps). It is a way of looking, applied as a display filter over the canvas: nothing
in the figure changes, exports are untouched, and it lasts for the session. Use it while choosing
series colours or a colormap; a pair of series that merge under deuteranopia need a different pair.

# Drawing

The shape tools do what you expect; the **pen** (P) is placement-assisted: click to place
points; a ring appears when you're close enough to your first point to **close** the shape;
**Shift** constrains segments to 0/45/90°; dashed guides snap to alignments with earlier
nodes, and tick marks snap **equal edge lengths** — perfect squares and 45-45-90 triangles
from sloppy clicks. **Enter** finishes an open curve; while the background grid is showing,
the pen snaps to its vertices.

**Double-click a path** (or press **Enter** on it) to edit its nodes. Inside node-edit:
**v** moves nodes (**Shift+drag** constrains along the axes or the flanking tangents),
**p** continues drawing — connect to an endpoint to extend or merge the path — **d** deletes
nodes, and **Ctrl+drag** on a segment **bends** it. The Inspector's *Closed path* checkbox
opens or closes any path.

# Arranging text in its box

Press **T**, then either **click** for a label — the box hugs whatever you type on one line —
or **drag** out a box for a paragraph: the text wraps at the width you drew and the box grows
downward as you type. Every text box has a **sizing** mode you can change later — *Auto*
hugs, *Auto H* wraps at the box width and grows downward, *Fixed* keeps both dimensions — and
everything below arranges the text **inside** that box.

**Align** places the lines across the box: *Left*, *Center*, *Right*, or *Justify*. Justified
text stretches every line out to both edges by widening the gaps **between words** — the
letters keep their own spacing — and leaves the last line of each paragraph at its natural
width, the way a printed column does. A line holding a single long word is left alone, since
there is no gap to widen. It needs a width
to fill, so choosing it on a hugging label turns the label's current width into the box's
width (*Auto H*): nothing moves yet, but drag the box narrower — or keep typing — and the
lines wrap and fill it.

**Vertical** places the block down the box: *Top*, *Middle*, or *Bottom*. The box itself never
moves or changes size — only the text inside it does. There is nothing to see until the box is
taller than the text, so this row appears with *Fixed* sizing (a hugging box is exactly as tall
as its text). It is what lines a label up with the middle of the panel beside it.

**Line height** is the distance between lines, as a multiple of the font size (1.2 by default —
1.5 reads more airily, 1 sets the lines tight). **Paragraph space** adds extra room before each
new paragraph, so you can separate paragraphs without leaving blank lines; it counts only where
you pressed Enter, never between the lines of one wrapped paragraph. **Tracking** is letter
spacing — the space added after every letter. Both are in **points**, like the font size, and a
negative tracking pulls letters together. Tracking changes how much fits on a line, so a
wrapping box re-wraps as you adjust it.

**Halo** puts a ring of the background colour behind the letters, so a label stays readable where
it crosses a plot's lines or an image (the 3Blue1Brown backstroke). Set its width in pixels (0 turns
it off); it takes the figure's or slide's background unless you pick a colour. It shows in the
editor, in exported figures and papers, and in slides; PowerPoint text boxes have no halo.

**Italic for one word, not the whole box.** Double-click the text to edit it, select the part
you want — a species name, a gene symbol, a single letter — and press **Ctrl+I**, **Ctrl+B** or
**Ctrl+U**. Only that stretch changes; the box keeps its own font, so the rest of the label is
untouched. With nothing selected, while you are typing, the same keys style only what you type
next: press **Ctrl+I**, type the species name, press **Ctrl+I** again and carry on upright. Moving
the cursor or clicking ends that. To style the whole box, click the box without editing it, or
select all of its text first. The formatting sticks to the letters it was given: type in the middle of an italic word and the
new letters are italic too, type against its edge and they are not, and deleting the word takes
its formatting with it. The formatting shows on the canvas as you work. Bold makes letters
wider, so after a bold word the text cursor can sit a few pixels off the letters. In the rare
case where a bold word pushes text onto another line, the box shows plain text while you type,
and the bold appears when you click away. (**Escape** throws the whole edit away, formatting
included.)

**Superscript and subscript.** Select the characters and press **Ctrl++** (superscript) or
**Ctrl+=** (subscript), or use the Inspector's **X²** and **X₂** buttons. The characters are set
smaller and raised or lowered, so *x²* and *H₂O* stay in one text box. **Ctrl+.** and **Ctrl+,**
do the same, as in Google Docs. Pressing the same one again puts the characters back on the line,
and with nothing selected it applies to what you type next, like the other styles.

**Color and the Inspector work on the selected letters too.** While letters are selected, the
Inspector's Text section says *Styling N selected characters*. Its **B**, **I** and **U** buttons
then format just those letters, and you can press several in a row. The *Text* color swatch
paints just those letters as well, so one symbol can be red inside a black label. Click
**Whole box**, or click the canvas, to style the whole text again. A colormap gradient always
covers the whole box, so it is not offered for a few selected letters.

All of these sit in the Inspector's Text section and in the **F** menu, they apply to every
selected text at once, and each adjustment is one undo step. A **named text style** (the
Inspector's *Style* row) carries them too, so "Panel body, justified, 1.4 line height" becomes
one click on every label in the figure — and editing the style restyles every text linked to
it.

# Cascade

Select several things and press **Ctrl+Shift+C**: the **cascade** popover applies a *stepped
delta* across the selection — each object offset a bit more than the last. Pick the property
(position, rotation, opacity, size, stroke width, font size, or a color), the step (add or
multiply), and the ordering (selection, layers, left→right, top→bottom); colors ramp
perceptually in OKLCh (ΔL/ΔC/ΔH per step). The preview is live; **Enter** applies as one undo
step, **Escape** puts everything back. Fanned annotations, graded palettes, staircase layouts —
one gesture.

# Panels and captions

- Mark a text element as a **panel label** with **Alt+L** or the **Panel label** toggle
  in its **F-menu**; **Auto-letter panels** (in the
  Inspector's Figure section) letters them a, b, c… in reading order.
- Panel references follow the panel itself when you relabel or auto-letter panels. Flux updates
  saved manuscript references and open editor buffers automatically. If removing a referenced
  panel would make its reference point somewhere else, the save stops with a clear conflict
  until you restore the panel or repair that reference.
- **Alt+M** opens **Figure-Meta** in Figure or Paper, starting with the active figure.
  Browse every canvas, search and filter families, and edit the **Captions** or **Name** tab.
  The figure and composed caption preview sit beside the fields; drag the divider to resize
  them. The Name tab includes family, number, title and custom families. Existing captions
  and permanent references are preserved. Captions flow into the [manuscript](paper.qmd)
  and exports automatically. Each field grows to fit; the fields column scrolls. Set the
  typing size with the **− / +** controls above the blocks (also in **Settings → Figure**).
  Click a block's letter or heading to collapse or expand it.
- The preview fits the entire figure **and caption** by default. **Ctrl-scroll** zooms around
  the pointer; drag to pan, choose a percentage, or press **Fit** to see everything again.
- **Add closing caption · ps** adds optional prose after the final panel caption. It appears
  as ordinary text, with no “ps” label, and stays at the end when panels are added or reordered.
  Remove it with its **×** button; metadata Undo can restore it.
- **Shift+Alt+M** opens Figure-Meta already pinned in a separate window; **Pin open** and
  **Dock** move the same view between windows. You can keep editing the workspace while
  it is pinned. **Shift+Alt+G** likewise opens the Plot gallery already pinned.
- **A** opens **Align & Arrange** with Align active; **Space** switches the active pane. **Alt+T** opens it with Arrange active.
  See [Alignment and arrangement](#alignment-and-arrangement) for spacing, anchors and plot spines.
- **Shift+R** shows rulers (drag from them for guides); **Shift+G** shows the background grid.

# Alignment and arrangement

Select objects and press **A** to open **Align & Arrange** beside them. Both panes stay
visible; click a pane or one of its controls to activate it. With Align active, click an
alignment button or use **W/A/S/D** for top/left/bottom/right. **H** aligns X centers along a vertical line;
**V** aligns Y centers along a horizontal line. Choose **Selection bounds**, a named
**Reference object**, or the **Figure** frame. One selected object aligns to the figure.
Each alignment is one Undo step; the panel stays open for further adjustments.

For semantic plots, **X spines** (**X**) aligns horizontal axes and **Y spines** (**Y**)
aligns vertical axes. The reference plot stays fixed. Whole groups move together, including
annotations. For multi-panel plots, use the panel and spine choices to identify the intended
axis. Unavailable spines are explained in the panel; ordinary alignment remains available.
These commands move plots without changing their domains, sizes or internal geometry.

Press **Space** on the tool surface to switch the active pane to **Arrange**, or open it
with Arrange already active using **Alt+T**. An existing row, column or simple grid keeps its order and internal offsets while
uneven gaps are tidied. A regular arrangement stays where it is. An ambiguous selection gets
a **Suggested grid** preview. Explicit **Row**, **Grid** and **Column** buttons reflow the
selection into centered cells; **A** toggles row/column, **G** chooses a balanced grid, and
**D/F** increases/decreases the row count.

Selecting an already evenly spaced row, column or simple grid shows pink gap guides without
opening the panel. This recognition leaves the objects unchanged; ambiguous overlaps do not
show guides. Drag a guide directly to edit spacing as one Undo step.

Drag a pink gap guide to adjust all gaps on that axis, or enter, scroll or scrub a value in
the spacing field. Negative gaps overlap objects, which is useful for stacked traces or
waveforms. Values have no zero floor; very negative spacing can move successive tracks past
one another while retaining their members, sizes and stacking order. Right/down increases spacing; left/up decreases it. **Shift** adjusts faster and
**Alt** more finely. **Keep fixed** chooses which edge or center stays in place; a grid offers
nine anchor points. Click the small pin on the selection to open the same chooser without
opening the panel. Center is the initial default; your choice stays selected across selections
and tool visits in the current app session. **1/2/3** chooses start/center/end on the gap axis
you are editing or hovering; numeric fields retain normal typing. Choosing a different anchor
moves nothing until you change
the spacing, and the fixed point always uses the actual selection bounds, including overlap. Grid gaps measure the space between column/row tracks, so smaller
objects can have more visible clearance within their cells.

**Enter** or **Apply** keeps the Arrange preview as one Undo step. **Escape** cancels the
current drag or field edit first; another **Escape** restores the arrangement from when you
entered. Switching back to Align keeps the arrangement. Input fields retain normal typing;
**Enter** accepts a field, and keyboard-focused buttons retain normal **Enter/Space** activation.
Both panes remain visible, and their headings select the active keyboard commands. Middle-button and wheel navigation remain
available between edits. These tools set ordinary object positions; they do not create an
automatic layout that later moves newly added objects.

# Reusable designs

**Ctrl+P** opens your **preset library** — a personal, machine-global collection of styled
shapes, arrows, callouts, and whole groups (a badge, a labelled bracket), organized in folders,
inserted with a click. Save anything from the **F** menu's *save as preset*; a group preset
arrives as one unit you can move as one or ungroup.

# Exporting figures

The Inspector's Export section renders the selected figure to **PNG**, **SVG**, or **PDF** —
or, for submissions, expand **Journal-spec raster** and pick a target width (single/double column
presets or custom mm), a DPI, transparency, and export TIFF or PNG at exact print size.
An export captures the figure when you start it, so edits made while choosing a filename
cannot change its artwork or dimensions. Large raster exports offer **Cancel export** and
keep the editor responsive. An unsupported output size reports an error rather than reducing
its resolution. PDF pages use the figure’s physical dimensions.

**Send to deck…** turns the figure into a [slide](slide.qmd), still linked to the same plots.

# Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause → fix |
|---|---|
| Ctrl+click won't select a part | The plot isn't semantic (imported without its manifest) → re-save via `fp.save` and re-import, or check `flux validate-plot` |
| An import landed huge / outside the frame | True-size import of a large plot → **Ctrl+Shift+I** to bring it inside, then resize deliberately |
| My plot stretches instead of reflowing | Read the Layout status. Regenerate legacy plots with fluxplot ≥ 0.4; choose Reflow if Stretch was selected. Unsupported layouts name their reason. |
| Ticks look crowded | Enlarge the plot or reduce Content scale; fixed date/category/custom labels do not retick. |
| A label moved oddly | Check the Layout status and source transform. Use Stretch for a positional fallback, or correct the source annotation and regenerate. |
| Restyles vanished after regenerating | The plot's series names changed in the script → keep `series=` names stable ([why](../concepts/semantic-plots.qmd)) |
| I see a grey 3D tile | Read the message inside it. Restore a missing GLB, or enable graphics support if rendering is unavailable. Saved posters can still display when a new render cannot be made. |
| Orbit won't start | A notice says why: the model is locked or hidden (unlock or show it), its file is missing, rendering is unavailable, or another editing mode owns the interaction. Resolve that condition, then choose Orbit again. |
| Saving says a 3D model file is missing | The model's GLB was moved or deleted from the project's `fig/assets/` folder. The figure still opens with a grey tile in the model's place, and saving waits. Put the named file back and save again, or select the model and delete it: saving resumes and the rest of the figure is untouched. **Ctrl+Z** brings the model back, and saving waits again until its file returns. If the message says a deck still uses the file, restore it or delete that model from the deck. |
| The labels look different in the notebook | The interactive viewer uses browser fonts; the PNG fallback uses Python's font renderer. Install the same font in both environments. Placement and point sizes remain explicit. |
| An untrusted notebook output is blank | VS Code can suppress an entire mixed HTML/PNG output. Trust the notebook if appropriate, or execute `sc.show(static=True)` to request only the PNG. |
| "These figures changed on disk" banner | Another tool or agent edited them → **Reload theirs** or **Overwrite with mine** — nothing is lost silently |

| “Some figures could not be loaded” | A referenced canvas is missing or unreadable. Restore or repair it and reopen the project; saving is blocked to preserve the existing files. |
| “Caption edits conflict” | Both the caption and its Markdown copy changed. Reconcile those versions before saving; changing panel labels alone does not create an external edit. |
